segments.title: 움직임에서 지금의 속도를 읽기
segments.text: A character runs forward, stops, and comes back. How much of that motion can we learn from only the starting and finishing positions? We will first record position and time with consistent units, then move from an average over an interval to the rate of change at one instant. Finally, we will combine the slope of a path with travel speed to calculate how quickly the character gains height.

segments.title: 이번 운동학의 범위
segments.text: The first question is where the object was at each time. That is a question of kinematics. Dynamics asks why it moved and which forces caused the motion. Here we represent the object as a particle with a position and temporarily set aside heat, electricity, fluids, and its own orientation or rotation. Our goal is to connect the meaning of differentiation to the simple calculation rules needed for motion.

segments.title: 단순화와 에너지의 역할
segments.text: A simplified model does not make the omitted ideas useless. Energy conservation can simplify motion problems and reveal a simulation that gains speed for no physical reason. Newtonian formulations emphasize forces, while Lagrangian formulations use energy-based quantities. We begin with the relation between position and time. The choice of formulation does not establish a universal rule that one handles friction better in every problem.
segments.screenPlan: 현재 입자 궤적 유지. 에너지 변화는 실제 측정하지 않은 게임값으로 표시하지 않고 해설용 진자/곡선의 보조그림. 비교문장은 조건과 목적 중심.

segments.title: 연속 모형과 프레임 계산
segments.text: We use a mathematical model in which time and position vary continuously. A computer evaluates it at discrete frames, but the equation describing the motion can still be continuous. We do not need a conclusion about the fundamental structure of spacetime. We assume a shared time coordinate, Euclidean space, and specified initial conditions and motion rules. Errors caused by finite time steps or numerical precision belong to the implementation and must be distinguished from the model.

segments.title: 입자로 시작하는 이유
segments.text: A particle in this model has mass but no size or orientation. That does not mean a character literally becomes a point; it means we track the position needed for the question being asked. We can understand motion along one line and then extend the calculation to horizontal, vertical, and depth components. Rotation and collision shape require additional information when those properties become relevant.

segments.title: 길이·시간·질량의 기준
segments.text: Before recording a position, we need consistent units. Mechanics uses length, time, and mass as basic quantities; we will generally use meters, seconds, and kilograms. Mass measures inertia, the resistance to changing motion. Weight is a gravitational force and changes with the gravitational field. Mass is measured in kilograms and weight in newtons. Even in a game with constant gravity, substituting one for the other breaks force calculations.

segments.title: 단위로 식의 의미 읽기
segments.text: Combining the basic quantities gives the units of other quantities. Area is length times length, measured in square meters, and volume uses three length factors. Velocity divides displacement by time, giving meters per second. Acceleration divides a change in velocity by time once more, giving meters per second squared. The symbols L, T, and M describe these dimensions independently of the particular measurement units.

segments.title: 진동수와 올바른 기호
segments.text: Frequency counts events per unit time. An event count contributes no length or mass dimension, so frequency has dimension inverse time. One hertz is one event per second, and one kilohertz is a thousand hertz, written kHz with a lowercase k. Similarly, force has units kilogram meters per second squared, energy is newton meters, and power is joules per second. Writing energy as newton square meters introduces an extra length factor and is incorrect.

segments.title: 차원 분석으로 코드 점검
segments.text: Keeping units throughout the calculation provides a built-in check. Velocity times time produces a displacement in meters. But treating milliseconds as seconds makes the result a thousand times too large. Sixteen milliseconds is 0.016 seconds. At three meters per second, that interval produces a displacement of 0.048 meters. Checking whether the resulting dimensions match the intended quantity is dimensional analysis.

segments.title: 단위 변환의 한 단계
segments.text: Unit conversion uses the same idea. To convert 14.57 meters to feet, multiply by about 3.28084 feet divided by one meter. The numerator and denominator represent the same physical length, so the factor does not change the quantity. Meters cancel, leaving approximately 47.80 feet. Following the cancellation of units makes the direction of the conversion clear.

segments.title: 여러 단위를 차례로 바꾸기
segments.text: Now convert 188 kilometers per hour to feet per second. Replace one hour with 3,600 seconds, one kilometer with 1,000 meters, and meters with feet. There is no need to memorize the complete chain: place each unwanted unit on the opposite side of a fraction so it cancels. Hours, kilometers, and meters disappear, leaving about 171.33 feet per second. We are now ready to describe the same motion in consistent units.

segments.title: 빠르다는 말의 두 뜻
segments.text: With units settled, return to motion. A hare runs quickly but sometimes moves backward or rests, while a tortoise advances slowly and steadily. A position-versus-time graph separates being fast at a particular moment from arriving first. Time is horizontal, and signed position is vertical. A high point means the runner is farther along; a steep segment means position is changing rapidly.

segments.title: 평균속도 정의
segments.text: Average velocity is the final position minus the initial position, divided by elapsed time. The signed position change is displacement. The symbol delta denotes a change: delta x is the change in position, and delta t is the time interval. For example, moving from two meters to eight meters in two seconds gives a displacement of six meters and an average velocity of three meters per second.

segments.title: 그래프의 기울기
segments.text: This ratio is the slope of the straight line joining the two points on the graph. It divides the vertical change by the horizontal interval. Even when the hare slows down, the line between the endpoints gives one average velocity for the whole interval. That number does not describe every event in between, so its start and end times must always be specified.

segments.title: 평균속력과 왕복
segments.text: Average speed instead divides total distance traveled by elapsed time and cannot be negative. Traveling six meters forward and six meters back gives twelve meters of distance but zero displacement. Over four seconds, average speed is three meters per second while average velocity is zero. Resting and making a round trip can therefore have the same average velocity. If the hare and tortoise share the same starting and ending positions over the same interval, their average velocities are also equal.

segments.title: 지금 이 순간은 어떻게 구할까
segments.text: If an average hides the motion inside an interval, how can we obtain the velocity right now? At a single instant both changes are zero, so direct substitution gives zero divided by zero. Instead, choose a short interval starting at that instant. A straight position graph has the same slope over every interval. On a curved graph, shortening the interval lets us examine the motion increasingly close to the chosen instant.

segments.title: 하나의 위치 함수를 정하기
segments.text: Let the slowing hare have position x(t) equal to minus t squared plus six t minus one. In this illustrative model, time is in minutes and position in furlongs. At one minute the position is four furlongs, and at three minutes it is eight. We want the velocity at 2.5 minutes, when the position is 7.75 furlongs. Evaluating the position a little later gives an average velocity over a short interval.

segments.title: 짧아지는 구간의 수치
segments.text: First use half a minute, ending at three minutes. Position increases from 7.75 to eight, so 0.25 divided by 0.5 gives an average velocity of 0.5. With an interval of 0.1 minute, displacement is 0.09 and the average is 0.9. At 0.01 minute the average is 0.99, and at 0.001 minute it is 0.999. As the interval shrinks, the slope of the line joining the points approaches one.

segments.title: 극한과 접선
segments.text: We have not actually divided by a zero time interval. We examined the value approached as a nonzero interval tends to zero. That approached value is the limit. The secant joining two points tends toward the tangent at one point, and the tangent slope is instantaneous velocity. On a computer, making the interval excessively small can amplify floating-point error, but the mathematical definition uses the limit.

segments.title: 도함수는 새로운 함수
segments.text: This definition is not limited to position. A derivative describes how rapidly an output changes when its input changes. Differentiating position with respect to time gives a velocity function. The result is not necessarily a single number: first we obtain a new function that returns velocity for a supplied time, then substitute a time such as 2.5 minutes to obtain a particular value. Distinguish the rate-of-change function from its value at one instant.

segments.title: 같은 위치에서도 방향은 바뀐다
segments.text: Comparing position and velocity makes the distinction clearer. In a model with initial velocity three meters per second and acceleration minus one meter per second squared, the tangent becomes horizontal at three seconds. Velocity is then zero; afterward, the object moves back even while its position remains positive. By four seconds, displacement is four meters, but the object traveled 4.5 meters forward and 0.5 meter back, totaling five meters. Direction comes from the graph’s slope, not the sign of position.

segments.title: 비와 압력의 변화율
segments.text: The same tool measures changes other than motion. The derivative of accumulated rain-gauge height describes how quickly rain is accumulating now. Tank pressure can also be recorded over time. If temperature and volume are fixed and the ideal-gas approximation applies, pressure is proportional to the amount of gas, so its rate of change indicates the rate of inflow or outflow. That interpretation depends on those conditions.

segments.title: 시간이 아닌 입력을 미분하기
segments.text: The input need not be time. If terrain height is a function of horizontal position, its derivative gives the local slope: positive uphill, negative downhill, and zero on level ground. Now consider the proportion of climbers who reach a specified height. That proportion decreases with height, so its derivative is negative. A large negative magnitude indicates many climbers dropping out near that height; a value near zero indicates few.

segments.title: 부호와 가상의 한계효용
segments.text: If fewer climbers drop out after a rest ledge, the negative derivative moves closer to zero; its numerical value increases rather than decreases. A change from minus ten to minus two is an increase. Actual counts form steps, so this interpretation uses a smooth approximation. A hypothetical satisfaction-versus-income curve works similarly: its derivative measures the effect of one additional unit of income, an example of marginal utility. The illustrative curve is not survey evidence.

segments.title: 평균 변화율에서 미분의 정의로
segments.text: These examples share one definition. Call the current time t and a nearby time t plus h, so h is the time interval. Divide the change in position by h to get the average velocity over that short interval. If this ratio approaches a single value as h approaches zero, that limit defines instantaneous velocity at t. We do not substitute zero into the denominator. We take the limit of ratios formed with nonzero intervals.

segments.text: Apply that definition to our position function, minus t squared plus six t minus one. To evaluate the position at t plus h, replace every t in the function with t plus h. Then subtract the entire original position at t. The minus sign before the second bracket applies to every term inside it. Keep h nonzero while simplifying.

segments.title: 전개와 약분이 필요한 이유
segments.text: Expanding the square cancels the t-squared terms, the six-t terms, and the constants. The numerator becomes minus two t h minus h squared plus six h. Every term contains h, so for nonzero h we can cancel it against the denominator. What remains is minus two t minus h plus six. Taking h toward zero now gives minus two t plus six: the velocity function for any time in this model.

segments.title: 한 점의 답과 함수 전체의 답
segments.text: At t equal to two point five, velocity is one, matching the value approached by our short-interval calculations. At two minutes it is two; at two point four it is one point two; at two point six it is zero point eight; and at three minutes it is zero. As tangents on the position curve flatten, the velocity graph falls. After three minutes velocity becomes negative, and position decreases.

segments.title: 그래프에서 읽는 규칙과 꺾인 점
segments.text: A position graph now tells us about velocity. A horizontal section means rest, an increasing section means positive velocity, and a decreasing section means negative velocity. A straight segment has constant slope and constant velocity; a curved segment has changing velocity. A sharp corner is different: if left and right slopes disagree, the derivative does not exist there. An idealized instantaneous change of direction in a game must handle that discontinuity separately.

segments.title: 미분하면 사라지는 정보
segments.text: There is another important loss of information. Moving a position graph vertically does not change its slope. Two objects that start at positions zero and ten but move identically have the same velocity function. Differentiation retains the rate of change but removes a constant position offset. That is why recovering position from velocity later requires a starting position.

segments.title: 서로 다른 미분 표기 읽기
segments.text: You will see several notations for the same operation. d x over d t means differentiating position x with respect to time t. The operator d over d t placed before a function tells us to differentiate that function. A prime also denotes a derivative, while a dot above x often means a time derivative in mechanics. For a general function of x, we write d y over d x. The variable below tells us which input is changing.

segments.title: 매번 극한을 계산하지 않는 규칙
segments.text: We do not need to repeat a limit calculation for every function. Standard differentiation rules let us break complicated expressions into simpler parts. Start with a constant function. If its value remains k as time passes, its graph is horizontal and its derivative is zero. Whether k is three or one hundred makes no difference. The question is whether the value changes with the input.

segments.title: 합과 상수배: 기차 안의 사람
segments.text: The derivative of a sum equals the sum of the derivatives. Imagine a person walking forward inside a train traveling along a straight line. Relative to the ground, the person’s position is the train’s position plus their position inside the train. Their ground velocity is therefore the sum of the two velocities: ten meters per second for the train plus two inside it gives twelve. Here we use aligned, nonrotating axes along a straight track.

segments.title: 단위 환산도 상수배로 미분하기
segments.text: If a function is multiplied by a constant, its derivative is multiplied by the same constant. Converting a position from furlongs to meters multiplies it by two hundred one point one six eight. The derived velocity gets the same conversion factor. Preserving sums and constant multiples is called linearity. It lets us differentiate a polynomial one term at a time and then add the results.

segments.title: 거듭제곱 미분 규칙
segments.text: For t to the power n, multiply by n and lower the exponent by one. The derivative of t cubed is three t squared, and that of t squared is two t. For a quartic polynomial, apply the rule to each power and remove the constant term. The rule also works for negative integer powers on their domains, but a denominator involving t excludes zero where the original function is undefined.

segments.title: 다항식 두 예제와 역수 예제
segments.text: Apply those rules in order. Three t to the fifth minus four t becomes fifteen t to the fourth minus four. For t to the hundredth divided by one hundred, the factor one hundred from differentiating cancels the denominator; the added square root of pi is constant and disappears. For reciprocals, rewrite the powers as negative exponents. The derivative of t to minus one is minus one over t squared, while four t to minus three becomes minus twelve over t to the fourth.

segments.title: 다항식에서 사인과 코사인으로
segments.text: Games also use sine and cosine for rotations and oscillations. Maclaurin series connect these functions to polynomials near zero. Sine begins with x, minus x cubed over three factorial, plus x to the fifth over five factorial, and so on. A factorial multiplies the positive integers up to its argument: three factorial is six and five factorial is one hundred twenty. The angle x must be in radians.

segments.title: 근사 오차와 급수의 조건
segments.text: Using the first four terms for inputs with magnitude at most one gives an error no larger than the next term, one over nine factorial, about two point seven six millionths. At x equal to zero point five the approximation is about zero point four seven nine four two five five three three. Adding terms brings the curve closer to sine. Not every function equals a power series, and software libraries need not use this particular formula. This example connects familiar polynomial rules to trigonometric functions.

segments.title: 사인의 미분이 코사인이 되는 연결
segments.text: Differentiate the sine series term by term. x becomes one. Minus x cubed over three factorial becomes minus x squared over two factorial. The fifth-power term brings down a five that cancels the five in five factorial, leaving four factorial. The resulting series is the cosine series. Differentiating cosine gives minus sine. With radians, sine’s slope is cosine and cosine’s slope is minus sine.
formulas: d(sin x)/dx=cos x; d(cos x)/dx=−sin x

segments.title: 자기 자신을 변화율로 갖는 함수
segments.text: The exponential function has a related property. The series for e to the x begins with one, x, x squared over two factorial, and so on. Differentiating removes the first constant, but shifts every remaining term forward, recreating the original series. The derivative of e to the x is therefore itself. This is why the function appears in continuous growth models whose rate is proportional to the current amount.

segments.title: 비례 성장과 조건
segments.text: For a quantity P growing continuously at a constant proportional rate r, its value is the initial amount times e to the r t. Here r is the growth rate per unit time. This is a mathematical continuous-compounding model, not a statement about a particular financial product. Nor is e to the x the only function equal to its derivative: any constant multiple also has that property. An initial value selects one specific solution.

segments.title: 안쪽 함수까지 함께 변한다면
segments.text: So far the function’s input has been x itself. A vehicle traveling over a hill has a nested dependence: time changes its position along the track, and that position determines its height. Let s be a path coordinate measured along the track, positive in a chosen direction. Height is a function of s, and s is a function of time. Nesting functions this way creates a composite function.

segments.title: 경사와 주행 속도를 함께 보기
segments.text: On the same hill, stopping the vehicle stops the height change. Moving forward faster changes height faster; reversing flips the sign. The vertical rate combines two factors: how much height changes per meter along the track, and how many track meters are traveled per second. Their product is height change per second. This is the chain rule. Because the first ratio uses actual path length, its magnitude cannot exceed one; it is not the usual rise divided by horizontal run.

segments.title: 단위로 확인하는 연쇄 법칙
segments.text: Suppose height rises by zero point two five meters for each meter along the track. At four track meters per second, height rises at one meter per second. The units confirm this: meters per meter times meters per second leaves meters per second. Reversing at four meters per second produces a vertical rate of minus one. Separating inner and outer changes makes the combined motion calculable.

segments.title: 사인 속의 입력부터 미분하기
segments.text: For sine of three x, differentiate the outer sine to get cosine of three x, then multiply by the derivative of the inner three x, which is three. For sine of x squared, the outer derivative is cosine of x squared and the inner derivative is two x. Multiply them. We are differentiating with respect to x here. If x itself changes with time, a time derivative needs another factor, d x over d t.

segments.title: 합성 함수가 여러 겹인 예제
segments.text: If the exponent is cosine x plus three x, the outer exponential remains unchanged and is multiplied by the inner derivative, minus sine x plus three. Finally, suppose the exponent is sine of three x plus sine of x squared. Add the two inner derivatives we just found: three cosine of three x plus two x cosine of x squared. Multiply that sum by the original exponential. Longer expressions still follow the same rule: preserve the outer input and include every inner rate.

segments.title: 출발점의 움직임을 다시 읽기
segments.text: We can now read the opening motion more precisely. Position differences between two times give average velocity, while motion at a particular instant comes from the tangent to the position graph. Differentiation turns that slope into a function. Power rules handled simple movement, trigonometric functions connected to rotation and oscillation, and the chain rule handled nested relationships such as a hilly track. The next question is how quickly velocity itself changes. That leads to acceleration, and then to integration, which accumulates motion back into position.
